Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Arguments: Arguments, Uncertainty: Uncertainty
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Mai was twenty-three when she nearly died on a stretch of highway she had driven a hundred times before. She had been merging into the left lane, music playing softly, when a pickup truck swerved into her path. She remembered the screech of metal, the violent spin, the world tilting as her car rolled. When it stopped, she was hanging upside down, blood on the dashboard, the smell of gasoline thick in her nose. She had no idea how long she hung there before the paramedics came. What she came to replay, again and again, was not the crash itself but the moment before—the way she had checked her mirror, the slight hesitation, the choice to accelerate instead of brake. If she had just waited two seconds, if she had honked, if she had done something different, none of it would have happened. That certainty settled into her bones like a second skeleton.

Over the following months, Mai’s world shrank. She stopped driving altogether, and her husband took over the commute. But it wasn’t just cars. She began to notice that her body felt dangerous—any physical exertion, even climbing stairs, made her heart race, and that racing felt like the beginning of the crash all over again. She started avoiding anything that put her body under stress: no gym, no running, no carrying heavy groceries. At work, where she managed database systems for a mid-sized logistics company, she found herself flinching every time a colleague raised their voice during a meeting. Arguments, even minor disagreements, sent a cold wave through her chest. She would sit frozen, convinced that the conflict would escalate into something catastrophic. Uncertainty became unbearable. A delayed email from a client, a missing file, an unclear directive—each one felt like a trap door about to open.

She stopped seeing friends, one by one. She had always trusted the people closest to her, but after the crash, she caught herself scrutinizing their intentions. What did they really want? Why were they calling? She began to believe that people would eventually let her down, that the only safe course was to keep them at a distance. Her husband, Lee, grew frustrated. He could not understand why she refused to go to dinner with their old college group, why she snapped at him when he asked her to pick up milk. She could not explain it, not in a way that made sense. What she knew was that she had failed to stop the crash, and if she could not stop that, how could she trust herself to manage anything else?

The memories would come without warning. Hearing someone say the name of the other driver in a story—a name she had learned from the police report—would send her pulse hammering. She began to avoid conversations where names might come up, and eventually, she stopped answering her phone altogether. When the thoughts pressed in too tightly, she would lock herself in the bathroom and press a fingernail file hard into her forearm until the physical pain drowned out the mental one. She had discovered that hurting herself gave her a few minutes of quiet. It was not about punishment, exactly—it was about stopping the loop. She never told Lee. She was certain he would see her as broken.

By the time she walked into the clinic, twenty-five years old and married for two years, Mai was exhausted. She had taken leave from her job after a confrontation with a supervisor over a routine database migration—an argument so minor she could barely recall the details, but it had sent her into a full day of trembling and self-harm. She had come to believe that she could not keep living like this, that something had to change. What she hoped, more than anything, was that someone could tell her whether the crash had truly been her fault—and that someone could show her how to stop being so afraid of her own body, her own husband, her own name.
